title: Kesones ohr with an alef: the garment of light, the tikkun and the refinement of Nogah
overview: This chapter explains the garment of light, *kesones ohr* with an alef, which Rebbe Meir's Torah writes in place of *kesones or*, the leather covering that G-d made for Adam and Chava. After the *tikkun* the *levush chashmal* is a garment that shines rather than hides the light. The *tikkun* comes from the new *MaH* of *Adam Kadmon*, and its source is the eighth king of *Tohu*, the *middah* of *yesod*, which is *Yosef*, the interpreter of dreams. Exile is compared to a dream, which repeats what a person thought about by day, and each person has a G-dly spark to impose meaning on his life. Letters alone carry little meaning; the 288 sparks that fell with the scattering of the letters are refined when they are put in the context of a G-dly soul with a mission. *Nogah* is light that shines in a dark place and also what stands out through contrast: a candle shines most in darkness, and a stone set in a coarse material shows its light by contrast. A refined garment becomes like a clear lens, and the *zihara elyona*, the upper light, is the light through which the *neshamos* see the *Shechina*.

sections.title: The garment of light with an alef: a garment that shines
sections.summary: Rebbe Meir's Torah writes kesones ohr, garments of light, with an alef. After the tikkun the garment can shine instead of covering the light. The tikkun comes from the new MaH of Adam Kadmon, and the eighth king of Tohu is its source.

blocks.text: Last class the letters were treated as vessels and garments, and the breaking of the vessels, which left the *chashmal* as a protective garment. This class moves to the *tikkun*: how *kelipas Nogah* can be turned to good. The most positive form of *kelipa* is, kind of, the *levush chashmal*, already fixed and used on purpose as a shield.

Rebbe Meir's Torah writes *kesones ohr*, garments of light, with an alef. The *kesones or* of Adam and Chava are the thick leather covering, the *chashmal* that wraps *Zeir Anpin* and *Nukva* down to their feet and hides the light. After the *tikkun* the garment itself can shine.

The *tikkun* is rooted in the new *MaH* of *Adam Kadmon*. In *kabbalah*, all the lights of the worlds emanate from him and become *levushim* over him, and he acts through them. He is kind of like the *yechida* in a person, which expresses itself in intellect, emotion and action. The first *kelim* were made from the openings of his face and broke into *Tohu*. The new light, which it says comes from his forehead, is the new *MaH*, and it fixes them.

This is the eighth king of *Tohu*, the source of the *tikkun*, as explained elsewhere. The Torah lists the kings of Edom who ruled and died, but of the last, *Hadar*, it says only that he ruled. Another place does say that he dies, so the Sages explain that he did not die: he became *Moshiach ben Yosef* and made the *tikkun*. So the eighth king is the *middah* of *yesod*, which turns *Tohu* into *tikkun*.

The *tikkun* comes in stages. We are born with the *nefesh habehamis* and the body, which at first challenge us and seem to oppose G-dliness. Once we mature and see from the deeper perspective of the *shem MaH*, we see the good in them, and they go from opposing G-dliness to enhancing it. It is kind of like experiment in science: you need a theory, but you have to test it, and the testing is really the source of truth. The physical body has *Hashem's* choice, the *bechira* of the *atzmos*, and when *Moshiach* comes it says the *neshama* will be nourished from the body. This is the advantage of physical *mitzvos*, which *Tanya* says are higher than the *neshama* that first moves a person to do them. So once they are properly refined, they can become better and sources of light.

sections.title: Yosef, the eighth king, and exile as a dream
sections.summary: The eighth king is the middah of yesod, which is Yosef, the interpreter of dreams. Exile is compared to a dream: its meaning comes from the dreamer's own thoughts, and each person has the spark of truth within to impose meaning on it.

blocks.text: The eighth king of *Tohu*, which repairs it, is also *yesod*, the *middah* that *Yosef* is. *Yosef* is an interpreter of dreams.

phrases.en: and this is coming from this inner wisdom of *Adam Kadmon* that's expressed on the forehead

phrases.en: and this is what it says that *Yosef* was *potair chalomos*, he interpreted dreams

phrases.en: and that's why *Yosef* was called *Avrech*: the simple meaning is that he was a leader, that Pharaoh appointed him as a leader, or, like Rashi says, that he was an *av* and a *rach*, both like wise, like a father, but he was young in years, as explained elsewhere

blocks.text: Exile is compared to a dream, which is like the thoughts of the heart of *Zeir Anpin*: you dream about what you thought about by day. If a person works hard at Torah and *avodah*, his dreams reveal them. A dream means nothing in itself, but since it resembles what the person wants, the interpreter looks in, finds what he really wants, and applies that to the dream.

In *galus* (exile), it says *Zeir Anpin* is in a state of sleep, called *dormita*, like dormitory, and the *mochin* have left. In exile we act on what we feel, going through the motions and reacting, with no understanding to guide us. In *geulah* (redemption) a person has an inner sense of purpose, and he actively shapes his life toward it.

Ups and downs remain, but with *mochin* a person is flexible. When the flood came, others could do nothing; Noach said, 'I'm going to build a boat,' and it was no tragedy for him. A person with *mochin* is no slave to circumstances: he can become, as far as possible, a master of his situation.

The letters of a dream can be made good, ordered and meaningful, from a real source. A dream is nonsense, but it can be given meaning, and then it is very powerful. In a similar way, in *galus* people can be hypocritical and do as they like. The world does not care, and a person can feel he may do whatever he wants. There are consequences to a degree, but that is the level of the dream of *galus*.

Doing what you want, not caring about consequences, is like your free choice, though there are consequences to a degree. But within a person is the G-dly spark, the source of truth. When he wants a life of meaning and purpose and imposes it on his life, that is the fixing.

This goes back to the *ratzon hamuchlat*. The source is the inner wisdom of *Adam Kadmon* on the forehead: the inner desire, as against the external desires that come from looking outside. An immature person tries to please parents and society, and can eventually become jaded; that stifling state is *galus*. *Geulah* is when each person is true to his inner G-dly essence, his *yechida*.

*Potair* is also made of the letters *tofer* and *pe-resh*, like sewing letters into a story, and it means beauty and interpreting. *Yosef* was called *Avrech*: the simple meaning is that Pharaoh appointed him a leader, or, as Rashi says, he was an *av* and a *rach*, both wise like a father and young in years. The *av* is *chachma*, which can impose this meaning.

Letters are marks or sounds with no meaning in themselves, and we give them meaning: that is the whole idea of language and symbols. Language is one of our greatest tools, letting us extend memory and pass knowledge down over generations. In the same way, physical *mitzvos* are imbued with meaning. The holiness and G-dliness come from a higher place, and when they are put into physical form they become very powerful.
blocks.title: Letters and language

sections.title: The 288 sparks and what the letters lose
sections.summary: The tikkun comes after the refinement of the 288 sparks that fell with the scattering of the letters. Letters alone carry little intellect, and their meaning depends on the understanding of the one who reads them.

phrases.he: והיינו אחר הבירורים דרפ"ח ניצוצין
phrases.en: this whole idea of the *tikkun* and the interpreting of the dream, this is all after we refine the 288 sparks

phrases.he: שנפלו גם כן עם פירור ופיזור האותיות
phrases.en: that fell together with the scattering, the crumbling and spreading of the letters

phrases.he: וכלים דתהו
phrases.en: and the *kelim* of *Tohu*

phrases.he: כנזכר לעיל, בשכל המצומצם באות הנפרד,
phrases.en: like we gave the example before, when you break a word down into its letters, each letter has a very, very small amount of intellect in it

phrases.he: ואז נקרא כתנות אור באלף.
phrases.en: and then, when we are able to recontextualize and repair the light that's hidden there, it becomes a garment of light

blocks.text: This is all after the refining of the 288 sparks, which fell with the scattering of the letters and the *kelim* of *Tohu*. When the *kelim* fall, the letters fall too, and some of the meaning is lost. That is the 288.

The *Arizal* works out the 288: 72 times four, one for each of the four Names, *Ayin Beis*, *SaG*, *MaH* and *BaN*. He goes through a system of *milui*: a *panim milui* spells the letters out, and an *achor milui* spells them the other way. For each Name, the system takes the spelling and its gematria, and the *achor* spelling and its gematria, and finds the level where the breaking happened. The highest such level, with everything below it, is counted; for the four Names together the total comes to 288.

The falling letters create our *nefesh habehamis*, our body and the physical world, and our perception of them becomes disjointed from meaning. But we still desire them, because they hold sparks of G-dly potential: we want to eat and want money because of that. When we see why we really care, and put them in the context of a G-dly soul with a mission, we refine the sparks. Once they are refined, it becomes a garment of light.

Each letter of a word, broken into its letters, carries very little intellect, and it loses its context and much of its meaning. Information theory, a branch of computer science and mathematics, works this way: bits, a zero or a one, combine into whole computer systems, and now we are starting to build AIs that turn words into numbers, with the relationships encoded. So there is an understanding embedded in language and symbols, and when we understand it more clearly, they become very powerful.

The same words heard by someone without understanding lose their meaning; for someone with wisdom they induce ideas. That is one of the reasons, for example, that to understand *Chassidus* a person needs to give *tzedaka* and do *mitzvos*: as the Alter Rebbe talks about in his introduction to *Tanya*, a person who is confused and spiritually in the dark cannot see the light that is in the *sefarim*.

Two people can read the same *sicha*, *maamar* or *sefer*: one gets it deeply and the other does not, and may come out with the opposite of its meaning or a skewed idea of his own. The real essence of all of the *pnimiyus haTorah* comes from seeing the G-dly spark in yourself, and that takes a certain refinement.

Once you see the G-dly spark in yourself, you see it in other people, and in these words too: 'Oh, this is what the Rebbe is talking about.' The opposite is someone looking to find fault, who takes the same words and twists them. That is true of anything, even the Constitution and the laws that people say protect us. They protect us only while people read and interpret them with a correct perspective and a conscience.

Once a person is willing to twist them, they are just paper and words, and mean whatever you want. So the real source of meaning is inside the person. This is why the *Torah shebaal peh* is not written down: it is not that writing it is forbidden, it is that it cannot really be written. Without a person who has the inner wisdom, a codified text deteriorates and loses its meaning. This is what happens with *aggadah*. The Rambam says it is written so that foolish people take it literally and make it foolish, while a wise person recognizes the depth in it.

A king hides treasures in the palace wall for his young children, so no one else takes them. He decrees that nobody may change the walls, but some bricks pop out in odd ways. When the children are old enough, they notice that something is there, and they find the treasures.
blocks.title: The king's treasure in the wall

blocks.text: Chazal's strange statements are there to make you feel that they do not make sense, to draw you deeper. One story shows it. Three people came to Shammai and then to Hillel, wanting to convert. The first would convert only on condition that he learn the written Torah alone. Shammai chased him away; Hillel converted him and taught him the alef-beis. The next day Hillel taught him the letters in reverse, that tav is alef. The student said, 'That is not what you taught me yesterday.' Hillel answered that if he believes this is an alef and this is a bet, he needs the oral law, because the writing has no meaning without a tradition. The other two were similar: one wanted to learn the whole Torah on one foot, one wanted to become a kohen gadol. Shammai chased all three away and Hillel accepted them, and it says that afterwards they all met and said that, because of Hillel's humility, they were brought under the wings of the Shechina.
blocks.title: Three converts and Hillel

sections.title: Nogah is light that shows up against darkness
sections.summary: Nogah is light shining in a dark place, which looks brighter there than in daylight. Our senses are tuned by contrast, and a light shows most against darkness. A refined physical thing, like a stone set in dark metal, shows its light through contrast.

phrases.en: and this is the idea of *kelipas Nogah*

עד שנראה אורו מבהיק ביותר מאור המאיר במקום אורה,
phrases.en: to your eyes, the light will seem brighter because you're in the dark than when you're sitting in a bright room

phrases.he: כמו שאמרו שרגא בטיהרא מאי מהני

phrases.en: because it's brightening, it's in contrast to the darkness

phrases.he: רק מצד החושך
phrases.en: It's that it seems brighter to our eyes, it has a bigger effect on us. It's because of the darkness that allows us to appreciate the brightness of the candle

phrases.he: שהוא היפוכו

blocks.text: Why is it called *Nogah*? It means something with a certain brightness, light that shines in a dark place. A little flashlight seems very bright in the dark but not in the daytime, because the light is brighter to the eye against darkness.

Our senses adjust to what is around us. Nerves can fire at different speeds, and the range between the slowest and fastest is tuned to the situation. In a bright place the eye adjusts to the brightness around it; in a dark room it readjusts over a few minutes, and after 15 or 20 minutes in the dark you see many more stars. So it is all about contrast.

In drawing and painting what matters is value, the division of the picture from brightest to darkest, not the color. A black and white or sepia photograph still reads, because the difference in value matters more than color. He once taught a class on growing plants: a room of lights seems bright to us, but it is a thousand times dimmer than sunlight through a window, and a plant would not grow under it without a very strong light close to it. We think it is bright enough, and do not realize it is actually very dark, because our eyes adjust.
The saying of *Chazal* asks, what good is a candle in midday? In a dark room a candle helps; outdoors it adds nothing to the brightness of the day.
blocks.title: The candle in midday

blocks.text: But a candle in thick darkness shines very brightly, because it lights up the dark, which is its opposite. The candle does not shine more at night in itself. It seems brighter to our eyes, and the darkness is what lets us appreciate it. By day we say we do not need a candle; at night we do.

This happens often. When times are good, in a yeshiva or a holy place, we think we do not need the childish little customs. That is the whole thing with Korach, who argued with Moshe: why does a garment need tzitzis if it is all techeles, or a house need a mezuzah if it is full of sefarim? That is kind of why we don't wear tefillin on Shabbos and Yom Tov: then we have the greater connection. Tefillin are for the weekday, out in the world, a small reminder like the candle, to focus us.
blocks.title: Why no tefillin on Shabbos

blocks.text: Many things look unimportant, but in a very dark place they bring light and become very important. In wars and in the Holocaust, every small *mitzvah* was precious: a *siddur*, a pair of *tefillin*, finding a way to light the *Chanukah* candles.

phrases.he: ואין זו הבהקה אמיתית מצד עצמו,
רק שנראה לעין בהבהקה יותר, מפני החושך דוקא, שבו בא יתרון האור לעין הרואה לבד
phrases.en: So when they're in the darkness, because they're in the darkness, so therefore they appear to the person with a much greater light

phrases.he: וזהו כמו הבהקת ובהירת אור האבן טוב, בהיותו מצוייר בגסות החומר,
phrases.en: And this is, for example, if you take a beautiful diamond, and if you set it into glass, you're not going to see it. But if you take the diamond and set it into something that's metal, that's opaque, or on black velvet, then it looks very brilliant, and you really see it shining because there's contrast

phrases.he: שהוא בהיר יותר משהוא מצוייר בחומר זך ובהיר
phrases.en: So you need the contrast between something very opaque and very dark, and something like a diamond that's very brilliant. The gemstone is going to appear much more beautiful and much more shiny than if you put it in crystal

phrases.he: כו' מטעם זה
phrases.en: It's like, no, that's not going to look nice, for this very reason.

blocks.text: In the darkness and the opposition, a person finds an inner strength and self-sacrifice that he did not know he had. Simple customs bring it out, and their value shows only in such situations.

In the Holocaust a girl's father left her with a non-Jewish family. When he came back she did not remember him, and he tried to make her know he was her father and she was Jewish. Colorful *Chanukah* candles, which he always bought, finally did it.
blocks.title: A girl and the Chanukah candles

blocks.text: Little things that seem childish or unimportant can have powerful effects: the songs from kindergarten, dipping the apple in honey, blowing the *shofar*. These very simple physical things can have a very powerful effect.
In the darkness the light appears to the eye with far greater force, because of the darkness itself.

A diamond set in glass cannot be seen. Set in something opaque, like metal, or on black velvet, it looks very brilliant, because the contrast shows the shine. A gemstone is more beautiful in a coarse material than in crystal, so you need the contrast. This is the first aspect of *Nogah*: a coarse, physical *kelipa* can, if refined and used properly, help you appreciate the light, because it provides contrast. Sometimes something very deep and spiritual, put in a physical form, is revealed through that contrast.
blocks.title: The diamond on black velvet

sections.title: Nogah has two meanings: shining, and standing out through contrast
sections.summary: Nogah means light that shines against darkness, and also something that protrudes and comes to the forefront. The sun in a cloud, the rainbow and a refined precious stone show how contrast reveals hidden detail, and how a refined material reveals what is inside.

Everything else becomes noise, and there is one clear signal. Without that, an intellectual idea is abstract and it is not clear what point you want to bring out.

*Nogah* has two meanings. The first is light shining in a dark place. The second is the sense of protruding, *lashon blitah lachutz*: a person who juts from the path, pronouncing Hashem's name, or the thought that stands out in the mind, as in *vehagita bo*, to meditate on it, and *vehegyon libi*, the thoughts of my heart.
Both meanings have the same *kavana*: something stands out and becomes apparent because of contrast.

phrases.en: It has to be a clear, refined stone, so that it can really shine, and that's one of the main things, they call it in a diamond like the fire: how it reflects the light back at your eye in a bright flash from many angles, and you get different colors from the different angles also

blocks.text: The class defines the term *Nogah*, used of the worlds, the *sefiros* of *Nogah* and *kelipas Nogah*. It has two meanings: something that shines, and something that stands out through contrast, as a feeling or thought comes to the forefront.

Perhaps the two meanings also relate to language. We often do not know what a feeling is until we have words for it, and putting a thought or a feeling into words gives self-awareness, so we can think about it consciously. Perhaps the two meanings correspond to the *or*, the light, and the *kli*, the vessel: the light shines like light in a dark place, and the vessels can protrude, like words of thought.

The light of the sun shines into a cloud. The light is concealed and reflected there, and you see it there more than you see the sun itself. In a clear sky with no dust, a beam of sunlight right in front of you is not visible. But a cloud lights up, because the cloud resists the light somewhat, and that resistance provides the contrast that makes it visible.
blocks.title: The sun in a cloud

blocks.text: A refined cloud does more than show the light in general: it reveals the subtle details and beauty hidden in the light.

The three colors of a rainbow are the appearance of *Nogah* in the *Maaseh Merkavah*, where the light around the chariot looked like a rainbow. A thick storm cloud blocks the sun; a light, fluffy cloud reveals the colors hidden in white light.
blocks.title: The rainbow in the cloud

blocks.text: A challenge can reveal talents you did not know you had. Putting words to things helps you find the differences in an idea or a feeling. Each *yom tov* and each *minhag* brings out a slightly different color of our connection to G-d, a different flavor. *Sukkos* is different from *Pesach*, and each brings out more love, fear and joy in its own color. Without a *kli* to bring it out, a person would never really experience it.
If the cloud is dark, it only blocks the light. The contrast shows you what you should not do and what you should do. You learn who you are from a situation that feels stifling: this is not who I am.
A person who sins and feels bad finds his *neshama* through the feeling. Otherwise he would think, 'I am always G-dly, I can do whatever I want.' That is one stage.

The next stage is that challenges reveal potential more deeply. The *midrashim* say that before the flood the atmosphere was thicker, so there was no rainbow. After it, people became refined and could grow and change through difficulties: that is the rainbow, the sign of *teshuva*. Before the flood people were too coarse to do *teshuva*, and the wicked were only contrast for Noach to be a *tzaddik*.

A precious stone, like a diamond or a ruby, does not look as nice in its colors on its own. It looks much more beautiful set in a physical material, but not a coarse one: a clear, refined stone that lets the light come through and reflects and refracts it in interesting ways. Like the fire of a diamond, it sends the light back to the eye in bright flashes from many angles, with different colors from different angles.
blocks.title: The clear stone

sections.title: Refinement: challenge, thought, self-awareness and the wings
sections.summary: A refined Nogah shows the light by revealing distinctions, in challenge, in puzzles and in thought put into words. Self-awareness is a double-edged sword, and the same tool can be an instrument of kedusha or a distraction, as with the wings of the Shechina.

blocks.text: The second meaning of *Nogah* is protrusion. In a very refined material, made somewhat transparent, the light stands out and breaks into its colors, revealing distinctions that were hard to see. The darkness is what lets the light show, and a challenge is what reveals it.

Once we master the challenges, the physical things, like the *nefesh habehamis* in our body, can reveal our spiritual potential more deeply. That is why we like puzzles and games: each one brings out part of our potential, and new skills.

There is a difference between a challenge that can be overcome and used as a springboard, and things that are completely bad. The Alter Rebbe, in prison, had chances to inspire people and sanctify G-d's name; someone else can be in a situation that is not like that at all. Even the Frierdiker Rebbe found prison pretty terrible. There are three impure *kelipos*, which are totally bad; their breaking is their repair. The Frierdiker Rebbe said that he would not spend another moment in prison for anything, but would not give up one moment he was there, because of the inner strength it revealed in him. So there is a silver lining, and there are things, like the bad before the flood, that are simply destroyed.

The same is true of abstract thought: putting an idea into the letters of a language makes its subtleties recognizable and tangible, and that brings out the depth of the understanding. Formalizing mathematics is like this: you take intuition and make it into logic and laws. That makes the spiritual tangible, and it is fruitful, because it forces you to clarify and to find implications you did not realize. Logic and mathematics are not a source of truth on their own; they uncover what your assumptions already contain, and they show contradictions. So putting a thing into words helps you understand it more than the experience or the intuition alone.
We have a *mitzvah* to learn Torah this way. Even if a person feels G-dliness, it is a *mitzvah* to put Torah into words and formalize it, because that brings clarity about what Torah really is.

blocks.text: A little kid does things without self-awareness. At a certain point we can be aware of how we are doing, whether we are smart, kind or mean. By creating ways of defining these things, we gain self-awareness.

That is the *yesh*, the ego or the substance of a thing that becomes felt and can protrude. It is not necessarily bad, but it can be a distraction: a double-edged sword, like the spinning sword that guards the way to the Tree of Knowledge.

Seeing oneself as wise in one's own eyes can be good or bad. A doctor should know he is a doctor and come to help, and knowing your abilities and deficiencies is the point of the *cheshbon hanefesh* of *Elul*. But a person who is wise in his own eyes is usually a little full of himself.
Nachor's concubine Reumah: Chazal ask her name, and answer *Re'u sheani batel*, look how *batel* I am. She was humble, but she knew it, and wanted everyone to know.
The joke: a yeshiva where everybody said 'I'm a worm, I'm nothing'. A newcomer said it too, and one guy turned and said, 'Oh, look who thinks he's a nothing.'

blocks.text: A person can have self-awareness of his *bittul*, and that can be good or a distraction. As children we have none. The *levush chashmal* is what parents tell us, 'do this, don't do that', and from it we gain our own self-awareness.

That self-awareness is a double-edged sword. It can be stifling, so that we just conform, or it can make a person a goody-goody who cares about the checklist. Or it can help me grow: tests should show my progress, as a coach tracks things, so I can challenge myself. That is the idea of *kelipas Nogah*.
A G-dly excitement that a person is very self-aware of, as in the *Kuntres HaTefilah*: we want to feel it in a real way, but not chase the feeling. A sincere feeling is the goal.
It can be a very powerful tool, and it can also be a distraction. That is where it can be refined: it can be *kesones ohr* with an alef, or *kesones or* with an ayin.

phrases.he: וכל זה שרש בחינת החשמל שנעשה מחיצוניות דבינה
phrases.en: And this is all the idea of the *chashmal* that comes from the external aspect of *binah*: you're taking these external things, and the parent, or the leader, or the *rav*, or whatever, you're creating a *levush* to help guide a person and protect a person, and give them self-awareness, like tests, rules and procedures, right

blocks.text: This is the root of the *chashmal*, which comes from the external aspect of *binah*: a parent, a leader or a *rav* creates a *levush* of tests, rules and procedures to guide and protect, and to give self-awareness.

This can be helpful, but it can become a *kelipah*. Employees just follow procedures; you need a reasonable person who says, 'That is against our policy,' when it makes no sense. Just think about what you are saying.

Sometimes a rule does not fit the person. A doctor looks at the chart of a very tall child, and the BMI comes out wrong; for people at the extremes, very tall or very short, the charts are not accurate, and you have to look at the person.

blocks.text: It is good to codify things, and it can help. But sometimes you need to use your *sechel*.
This is the double-edged sword of *Nogah*, the spinning sword: it can go up to *kedusha* and down to *kelipah*, helpful and holy, or a distraction. Used properly, it is the idea of the *chashmal*.

Like a mother spreading her wings over her chicks, which is called the wings of the *Shechina*. When it is used properly, all this is a good thing.

That is the source of the *neshamos* of *geirim*. There are two kinds: those from *kelipas Nogah*, the wings of the *Shechina*, and those with the *neshama* of a Jew. sections.title: The curtain between worlds and the translation of the Torah
sections.summary: The levush descends until it becomes a masach, the parsa that divides Atzilus from Beriah; Malchus breaks through it. Between one level and the next everything passes through a levush, which is why the Torah is translated into mitzvos below. Once the self is nullified, the felt yesh becomes bittul.

phrases.he: עד שמזה נשתלשל ויורד עוד להיות בבחינת המסך ממש,
phrases.en: then it goes down to become a *masach*, a curtain or a mask that separates

phrases.he: הנקרא פרסא המפסיק ומבדיל בין אצילות לבריאה כו',
phrases.en: And that's called the *parsa*, the curtain that separates between *Atzilus* and *Beriah*, like the king would sit behind a curtain in certain cultures

phrases.he: והמלכות בוקע המסך (כמו שיתבאר)
phrases.en: And *Malchus* bursts through the curtain, it penetrates this curtain, like we'll explain

blocks.text: Further down, the letters and the *levush* become a curtain: the *levush chashmal*, then the wings, then the *masach*, a curtain that separates, called the *parsa*, between *Atzilus* and *Beriah*. In some cultures a king sits behind a curtain.

*Malchus* bursts through this curtain. The letters and the *levush* become a barrier: every interface, like a language barrier, goes through the letters and the *levush*, and comes only by way of that.

This goes back to *Adam Kadmon*, who associates our essential inner desire, which is for oneself, with external things, so that it becomes a desire for the outside world. The same process happens from *Atzilus* to *Beriah*: the essence of being G-dly is translated into a list of the 613 *mitzvos*: do this, don't do that.

Torah is revealed in *Beriah* through the circumstances of the world and of people. The essential Torah of *Atzilus* applies in any world, which is why the *malachim* asked for it: being true to your G-dly essence applies in all times and places. It is plugged in through this *masach*.

phrases.he: אך ענין כתנות אור באלף,
phrases.en: but then, so that's the regular idea of the *levush* and the regular idea of *kelipas Nogah*, where it's something separate and it's *kesones or* with an ayin, and it's hiding the light

phrases.he: הוא אחר התיקון ובירור דבחינת נוגה דחשמל
phrases.en: This is after there's this *tikkun* and *berur* of the *Nogah* of *chashmal*

blocks.text: The covering still serves a purpose: it is a protective barrier and gives contrast, like creative constraints.

Creative constraints work this way: told to write a poem with no rules, a person does it badly; give him a meter and a rhyme, and the constraints bring out his creativity. Our restrictions in *Torah* and *mitzvos* are like the rules of a game: without rules you are not forced to grow, and you could change them whenever it is hard. That is why a classroom has rules, tests and grades: positive pressure to reach inside and find your potential, the idea of the rainbow.
That is one aspect. The covering is still not *kesones ohr* with an alef: it hides, constrains and resists the light.
Rebbe Meir wrote *kesones ohr* with an alef, the way things will be when *Moshiach* comes, after the *tikkun* and *berur* of the *Nogah* of *chashmal*.
This is when a *tzaddik* has refined his body and nature. The first two perspectives are like a child who needs protection and rules to keep him in line.

This is related to what is said, that when *Moshiach* comes, *mitzvos* will be *batel*. The Rebbe explains that nowadays we do *mitzvos* as an external command, and that is the *levush chashmal*, a protective garment.
When *Moshiach* comes we will appreciate the *pnimiyus* of the law and want to do it on our own, not as a command, but as the *giluy* of our *etzem*.

After this *berur*, *chashmal* means any protective system: procedures to keep people in line when they lack the maturity to know what to do. A parent says 'do this, don't do that', and the child asks why, not yet seeing the dangers.

A little child is told not to play with matches. Once a person is old and mature he can use them, because he has the wisdom to use them properly. This is a whole *sicha* on this topic, on the *Torah* of *Moshiach*, where the Rebbe explains many things.

blocks.text: Why now we *pasken* like *Beis Hillel*, and when *Moshiach* comes, like *Beis Shammai*. Are *chumros* good or bad? A *neder* seems bad, though a *chacham* can permit it. There are two kinds of restriction: one put on an immature person, which he feels as stifling, so you cannot impose too many on someone who cannot handle them.

In *halacha*, the *hiddur* of not eating before *havdalah*: the Alter Rebbe brings that a child may not be made to wait to eat until *havdalah*, because you may not cause him pain. A *hiddur* is done out of desire to show the beauty of the *mitzvah*. For someone not at that level, forcing it is torturing him.
So these days we pasken like Beis Hillel. A *neder* is for someone not yet mature enough to do right on his own, like not playing with matches: you need those restrictions, like a *levush chashmal*.

Once a person has the *pnimiyus* of *chachma*, he should be *mattir neder*. Instead he self-imposes care about safety, the *chumros* of Beis Shammai of the time of Moshiach, from his own *hiddur*. You need the maturity to appreciate them. A *levush chashmal* is a restriction put in place because a person does not yet have the *mochin* to be guided properly, so they have to protect the *middos*.

blocks.text: Once the *levush* of *Nogah* is refined, a person can reveal this essential *bittul*, the *MaH chadash* of *Adam Kadmon*. He realizes who he really is: his *nefesh elokis*, not his *nefesh habehamis*. He finds his *yechida*, and that inner *bittul* shines through his sense of self and his worldview.

Then he wants to do the right thing *behidur*, with beauty, and enjoys it. A little kid does not want to learn, so you give him homework. An adult who is mature is intrinsically motivated and learns for its own sake, *lishmah*. With that perspective the *levush* of *Nogah* is no longer stifling; it is a tool that helps him.

The source of the *tikkun* is that the felt *yesh* becomes complete *bittul*. The *Kuntres HaHispaalus* describes two general levels of *avoda*. The first comes from the body: it understands why G-dliness is good for me, by calculation, so it is self-serving, like a job done for money. That is the level of the *levush* of *Nogah*, which has friction.
A person may do it for reward and punishment, here or in *olam haba*. That is not *lishmah*: it is still motivated by a sense of self-interest.

When a person finds the inner *bittul* that comes from his *nefesh elokis*, as the Kuntres describes, he does it simply because it is the right thing: 'I'm a Jew, how could I not do it?' He feels the *ratzon Hashem*, and his sense of self becomes a transparent thing.

When the *yesh* itself is in a state of *ayin*, it is higher than the *ayin* of the *MaH* of *chachma*. In *avoda* the physical heart feels the *gilui* of the *yechida* as an inner *ratzon*, stronger than understanding. It becomes the person's nature, not a question he debates.
It is not a matter of question or debate: a Jew does *mesirus nefesh* from his *etzem*, not because of *chachma*.
A physical object made into a lens, for a telescope or a microscope, magnifies the light, because it is so refined that it no longer resists. It helps you see further than you otherwise would.

sections.title: The garment of light: a refined yesh, a lens, and the upper light
sections.summary: A garment of light is one whose own substance shines: the felt yesh of the physical becomes bittul, and it is then higher than the chachma that refined it. Like a lens, the refined garment reveals the light, the zihara elyona, through which souls see the Shechina. The tail of the class turns to procrastination and to the good that lies in a nature, and to the hero's journey.

blocks.text: Therefore it is called *kesones ohr* with an alef: a shining garment where the garment itself is one of light, as it says that G-d wraps Himself in light.

The *levushim* of the physical world, at first because of the breaking of the vessels, seem like an enemy fighting us. With the maturity to refine them, we see that they are G-dly, our allies, the *ratzon* for a *dira betachtonim*. Unrefined they can be corrupted; the point is not that evil is good, but that once refined it is revealed as good.

blocks.text: The Torah's light after the *berur* of *MaH* of *chachma*: after the *nefesh elokis* refines the body, the body elevates the *neshama*, since it reveals Hashem's *bechira* and the *etzem*, which is higher than the *nefesh elokis*. A big theme in *Chassidus*.

*SaG* is the name of *binah*, with the letters of *gas*, coarse; that is where the breaking happened. It begins as an understanding of G-dliness above *MaH*, but through the breaking it becomes coarse and hides G-dliness. G-d's inner intention is that we reveal G-dliness in the physical world.

After we refine the *BaN* of *Malchus*, the fallen sparks go back to their source, the *SaG* above *MaH*. Through the *berur* of the breaking we reach higher than the physical and higher than the spiritual.

A letter of the Frierdiker Rebbe says *Chassidus* is based on *davka*: G-d could have made a spiritual world but chose a physical one; could have given the Torah to angels but gave it to people; could have created us without a *yetzer hara* but chose one.

He could have created that all the nations of the world love us, and He created *davka* that they hate us. And tens of thousands of other *davkas* like this: all of them come from one *davka*, that Hashem wants the truth, and the ultimate purpose is that we do *avoda* and reveal our true essence.

sensitivity.publishable: He could have created that everything comes easily to us, and He created *davka* that it is hard. And tens of thousands of other *davkas* like this: all of them come from one *davka*, that Hashem wants the truth, and the ultimate purpose is that we do *avoda* and reveal our true essence.

blocks.text: We do not do it only because it is easy or our nature; it is our real G-dly essence, found through effort. *Tanya* describes the *nefesh elokis* as *nefichah bekoach*, a forceful blowing, like a flint that is struck: the real essence of a person is revealed when something takes effort.

blocks.text: This is the *zihara elyona*, the upper light: light refined to great clarity in a clear garment, like a lens. Through it one sees added brightness with the eye. It does not hide the thing; it reveals it.

Think of looking through a microscope for the first time at a whole world of tiny creatures in one drop of water, with an amazing beauty and complexity, or through a telescope at the rings of Saturn or the storms on Jupiter. It reveals the wonders of G-d's world that we cannot normally see.

The physical *levushim* of Torah and *mitzvos* reach higher than the *neshama*, as *Tanya* says. When we use our *machshava*, *dibur* and *maaseh* properly for Torah and *mitzvos*, they connect to the *etzem* of G-d, which is higher than the *neshama*. This relationship exists all over the *hishtalshelus*.

phrases.en: So, then that type of *levush Nogah* provides a benefit, like we said: the two levels of *Nogah* before it is completely refined, where it provides contrast

blocks.text: Before the *berur*, *Nogah* is concealing and darkening. Its only advantage is that the darkness gives the light contrast, so it looks brighter.
A garment of bright, shining light, like clear glass, is the *aspaklarya denahara*, the *zihara elyona*, through which souls see the *zivo* of the *Shechina* in *Gan Eden*, as is explained elsewhere.
So that type of *levush Nogah* provides a benefit, the two levels of *Nogah* before it is fully refined: like a candle in a dark room, or the rainbow, where it provides contrast.

Once it is completely refined, it is like seeing a superior light through the lens: the *aspaklarya denahara*, the *nevuah* of *Moshe Rabbeinu* and the perspective of the *tzaddikim*, where the physical world is refined enough to reveal G-dliness. The *neshamos* see G-dliness in *Gan Eden* through the Torah and *mitzvos* they did here. That is enough to understand.

The *berur* and *tikkun* of *Nogah* has three stages. First, *Nogah* only provides contrast and is dark. Once refined a little, it reveals our inner potential. Once completely refined, it gives a superior revelation, something new.

Is procrastination good? I don't think it is in its unrefined state; when a person properly understands and refines the nature, there is an aspect of it that is good. G-d creates everything with opposites, and the struggle of opposites reveals something greater. If we did not have the desire to be lazy, we would never innovate; we would never think, there must be an easier way.

blocks.text: G-d gives two *malachim*, the *yetzer tov* and the *yetzer hara*. The *yetzer hara* starts out corrupted, so we see it as bad; refined, it is really good. Both are the desire for a *dira betachtonim*, and they become powerful and beneficial once we understand them and put them in the right context.

blocks.text: Why does G-d make us need to eat, and why do we like food that tastes a certain way? When we understand the reasons, we can actively use that nature for good purposes. Those are important and positive things. That is the whole idea of the *mitzvos*.

blocks.text: The *mitzvos* are prepackaged, refined actions meant to train us. The goal is not only to follow instructions, which is the *levush chashmal*, but to internalize them: *bechol derachecha da'eihu*, in all your ways know Him, even includes *aveira*. *Chazal* bring examples where a person had to do something generally against the rules, and in that context it was right.

blocks.text: Eliyahu's contest on Mount Carmel, when he offered a *korban* outside the *Beis HaMikdash*, was necessary. Making such an exception takes depth of understanding, to know it is the right thing and not laziness or lack of commitment. The mechanics are a whole *sugya*: how it can happen through a king, the *Sanhedrin* or a *navi*, and the limits set by *halacha ve'ein morin kein*.

blocks.text: A person procrastinates, misses a deadline and loses a job. Is that good? Here there are two perspectives, *da'as elyon* and *da'as tachton*, which he likens to being inside or outside the story. From one, we look for specific outcomes and success, and in it there is good and bad.

blocks.text: A person does something bad and the outcome is bad. From a higher perspective, he can look back, appreciate the mistakes and enjoy the whole thing. A good story is not 'they lived happily ever after'. It is about a flawed person who failed because he would not face his real flaw, learned the hard way and changed. That is everyone's story and the world's.

blocks.title: A good story

blocks.text: When the story is over, the bad parts become good too, but only because they are bad. There are two kinds of good from the darkness: the good drawn out of it, which must be transformed, and the good seen in the darkness itself, which *Moshiach* will reveal. That second kind is part of the secret of the Torah, because at the wrong time it strengthens the evil.

blocks.text: Focusing on it at the wrong time stops a person from learning the lesson and growing, and he needs to learn it. After the fact, once he has learned the lesson and it is over, he can look back and see the good in everything. These are two different perspectives.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class .2 goes on past the chapter's last line to procrastination, the good in a corrupt nature and the hero's journey; placed under line 43.

blocks.text: The procrastinating nature has a great potential of good, revealed when the person masters and channels it. Procrastination is a corrupt form of a nature our *nefesh habehamis* has.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class .2 goes on past the chapter's last line to procrastination, the good in a corrupt nature and the hero's journey; placed under line 43.

blocks.text: Our *nefesh habehamis* has the *yesod* of earth, the source of laziness and procrastination. Refined, it becomes very good: steadfastness, refusing to change, so that a person would rather die than give up his true nature. The essence of each *yesod* is G-dly. Fire is the desire to change and grow; air is communication; water is enjoyment. Each has a corrupted form that leads to the *kelipos*, but it can be fixed and made good.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class .2 goes on past the chapter's last line to procrastination, the good in a corrupt nature and the hero's journey; placed under line 43.

blocks.text: Why did G-d create it in a corrupted state, as a challenge? That too is a deeper goodness: a person has to experience the bad thing and feel stifled. His *nefesh elokis* is distressed, and he suffers physically and spiritually. So he has to reach in and realize that this is not who he really is. That brings out the inner powers of his soul, and through them he makes the changes. That is the process of the refinement of *Nogah*.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class .2 goes on past the chapter's last line to procrastination, the good in a corrupt nature and the hero's journey; placed under line 43.

blocks.text: At the end, a person can look back and appreciate the challenge itself. The point is not that we will wish we could go back; it is that we will appreciate what we had in *galus* and cherish it.

blocks.text: This is the basis of every story, every book and every movie. They call it the hero's journey: learning and transformation, and coming back with a new perspective, with both kinds of good and bad in it.
